correctness.rationale: For all n>=2 and every i<j, the integer potential D partitions the pair set into consecutive nonoverlapping gap-pair intervals. Direct case analysis of the two letters shows exactly one outgoing transition reduces D by 1; every other transition leaves D unchanged or increases it. This proves exact shortest merging lengths and uniqueness without any finite-enumeration assumption. Rank residues give the explicit common suffix word in both parities. An independent reverse BFS for n<=80 and 10,666,600 supplemental potential checks through n=400 agree.

evidence: Behague–Johnson, arXiv:2008.12166, §1: universal bound RDV(2,n)=C(n,2) and a Černý extremal pair.
Their result gives the maximum over prescribed pairs and automata, not the individual distance map, strict all-distance multiplicities, or optimal-word uniqueness.
broader_coverage.reasoning: A sharp maximum does not determine the distribution beneath that maximum, or whether shortest words are unique. The current theorem reconstructs all pair lengths and gives a single word whose suffixes enumerate every optimum. Gusev’s odd-state structural diagram is the more serious possible implication and is described separately.

evidence: The known maximum C(n,2) follows immediately by taking the maximum of the claimed formula; this component is pre-existing.

Gusev’s odd-state transition representation could be used as a starting point to derive the odd instance, but it omits an even-state graph and does not publish the all-state explicit distance formula or uniqueness/suffix conclusion.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The new statement is stronger in information content than the established extremal value and expectation formulas. It also proves one-to-one rank occupancy and rigid word uniqueness for every pair, not just existence of a merging path. Residual risk: a reader may regard some odd-state portions as an elementary consequence of the earlier graphical representation.

evidence: Gusev, arXiv:1404.6731, §3 and Fig. 3: graph of odd-state pair automaton; probabilities of random absorption are the objects of the theorems.
The graph permits state-specific path computations but does not state the both-parity explicit distance bijection or common suffix-chain uniqueness theorem.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The claimed theorem is invariant under simultaneous cyclic relabeling only with a corresponding conjugation of the unique merging letter. Earlier odd-state pair graphs are closely related but only encode transitions; their published assertions are expected random times, not the complete deterministic shortest-word classification. The even parity and suffix-chain description are included explicitly here.

evidence: The inspected primary works present a pair automaton and maximum rendezvous value but no tabulation of all labeled-pair shortest-word ranks or uniqueness of all optima.
exact_database_or_table.reasoning: No exact all-pair table with the asserted bijection and suffix property was located; this is limited negative bibliographic evidence and not a uniqueness proof for the literature.

originality.rationale: The known general maximum two-state merging time C(n,2) and a Cerny extremizer are explicitly credited to Behague–Johnson (2020/2022), and Gusev (2014) gives the odd-state pair-automaton graph. Neither inspected work states the all-labeled-pair integer-bijection formula in both parities, or uniqueness and a common suffix chain of the shortest merging words. An earlier odd-state automaton representation is a genuine implicit-coverage risk rather than ignored evidence. No searched matching claim was located; a failed search alone is not the novelty argument.
residual_risks: The older odd-state pair graph may make part of the structural result implicit; statements equivalent under a different state labeling could be overlooked.
A published even-state complete pair-distance classification or unique-shortest-words result might be unindexed.

value.rationale: Prescribed-pair synchronization is a natural invariant in error recovery and rendezvous theory. The result determines every one of C(n,2) separate shortest distances, proves each length occurs once, and supplies a unique canonical optimum per pair as a suffix of a single explicit word for all n. This structural rigidity and complete distribution are more informative than the pre-existing maximum and are not an arbitrary numerical slice.
